person.name: Alvar_Aalto
person.tagline: Bent Birch Furniture and Finlandia Hall
person.summary: Alvar Aalto was a Finnish architect and designer who created buildings, furniture, glassware, and interiors. He developed a modern architecture that used natural materials, curved forms, and carefully designed furnishings. His projects ranged from Finnish public buildings to commissions in Europe and the United States.

events.title: Birth in Kuortane
events.description: He was born into a bilingual household in Kuortane, where Finnish and Swedish were spoken.

events.title: Studies Architecture in Helsinki
events.description: Aalto enrolls at the Helsinki University of Technology to study architecture. The Finnish Civil War interrupts his studies. He serves with the White Army at Länkipohja and Tampere. He graduates in 1921.
events.background:
Helsinki University of Technology trained architects through drawing, design exercises, and the study of historic styles. Usko Nyström taught architecture there from 1901 and remained on the faculty throughout this period. He taught ancient and medieval architecture, ornamentation, style history, and freehand and linear drawing. Nyström had studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and traveled widely in Europe on a state grant. His teaching brought the Art Nouveau, or Jugendstil, approach to several generations of Finnish architects. Aalto had already taken drawing lessons in Jyväskylä from the local artist Jonas Heiska before arriving in Helsinki.

While still a student, Aalto designed a house for his parents in Alajärvi. It was his first built work. In 1920 he made his first trip outside Finland. He traveled through Stockholm to Gothenburg and briefly found work with the architect Arvid Bjerke. The trip gave him direct contact with Swedish architectural practice during the years when Nordic architects were moving from National Romanticism toward a classicism based on proportion and traditional forms.

Aalto completed an independent design for the Industrial Exposition in Tampere in 1922. His early professional work continued to use the Nordic Classicist language common among Finnish and Swedish architects of the period. The bell tower of Kauhajärvi Church at Lapua dates from 1921 to 1923. His first office work in Jyväskylä included houses and local public buildings. In 1928, Aalto designed Nyström's grave marker for Hietaniemi Cemetery in Helsinki after winning a competition organized by the Finnish Association of Architects. The white-marble stone carries the words Bene latuit, a phrase quoted by René Descartes from Ovid: “The one who lives well, lives unnoticed.”

events.title: Opens Jyväskylä Office
events.description: Aalto returns to Jyväskylä and opens an architectural office in 1923. He calls it Alvar Aalto, Architect and Monumental Artist. He designs houses and local public buildings in the Nordic Classicist style.

events.title: Marries Aino Marsio
events.description: Aalto and architect Aino Marsio marry in Helsinki. They travel to Italy for their honeymoon. They study architecture together during the trip.
events.background:
Aino Marsio had qualified as an architect at Helsinki’s Institute of Technology in 1920. She was among a small group of women architects that included Salme Setälä. After working for Oiva Kallio in Helsinki, she moved to Jyväskylä in 1923 for a position in Gunnar Achilles Wahlroos’s office. She joined Aalto’s office the following year. The practice was then producing small houses and public buildings in the Nordic Classicist style. Young Scandinavian architects commonly traveled through Italy to examine vernacular buildings. That study helped shape Nordic Classicism during the 1920s.

Aino brought practical knowledge of woodwork to the office. As a child in a Helsinki cooperative apartment building, she had met neighboring master carpenters and joiners. She later apprenticed with them. Her work gave particular attention to interiors, furnishings, materials, and the comfort of domestic spaces. The couple’s early projects included small buildings and summer villas. Aino’s Villa Flora in Alajärvi, completed in 1926 and enlarged in 1938, was the first project credited entirely to her. It combined modernist efficiency with the simplicity of rural Finnish life.

Their professional work soon took them to Turku, where they collaborated with Erik Bryggman. The Aaltos entered some architectural competitions under separate names during their early partnership. They moved their office to Helsinki in 1933. In Munkkiniemi they designed a combined home and office for themselves in 1935–36. Aino concentrated especially on interior design, furniture, lamps, glassware, textiles, and household objects. She later served as Artek’s first artistic director and managing director. Under her leadership, Artek completed more than eighty interior commissions. Her pressed-glass series won a prize at the Milan Triennial in 1936.

events.title: Designs Viipuri Library
events.description: Aalto wins the 1927 competition to design the Viipuri Library in Viipuri. His proposal develops into a modernist design with roof skylights, wood finishes, and a wave-shaped auditorium ceiling.

events.title: Builds Paimio Sanatorium
events.description: Alvar and Aino Aalto design Paimio Sanatorium for tuberculosis patients. The building has separate wings and sunlit patient rooms. They design furnishings for treatment and rest.

images.caption: Paimio Sanatorium designed by Alvar Aalto
images.creator: V. K. Hietanen

events.background:
Finland’s architects were moving from Nordic Classicism toward Functionalism during the late 1920s. Functionalism was the Finnish name for the International Style of modern architecture. Aalto had traveled in Europe and followed the work of Le Corbusier, Walter Gropius, and other central European modernists. He also joined the Congrès Internationaux d'Architecture Moderne through the Swedish architect Sven Markelius. The second CIAM congress in Frankfurt took place in 1929. Aalto attended its fourth congress in Athens in 1933. His contacts there included László Moholy-Nagy, Sigfried Giedion, and the critic Philip Morton Shand.

The sanatorium project developed alongside two other major Finnish commissions. Aalto designed the Standard Apartment Building in Turku in 1928–29. That work gave him a chance to use concrete prefabrication. He designed the Turun Sanomat newspaper building in 1929–30 with a sharply modern form derived in part from Le Corbusier. He applied ideas from both projects to the sanatorium and to the long-running Viipuri Library project. The library had begun as a classical competition proposal in 1927. Financial problems and a change of site prolonged its construction for eight years.

Aalto had visited Jan Duiker’s Zonnestraal Sanatorium in the Netherlands while it was under construction. Historians have identified Zonnestraal’s spread-out wings as a source for the planning principle at Paimio. The Paimio work also gave the Aaltos an extensive interior commission. Aino concentrated much of her work on interiors and furniture in their shared practice. The furniture and lamps designed for the sanatorium occupied the Aaltos through 1933.

The best-known object from those interiors became the Paimio Chair. Its cantilevered form used laminated birch. Aalto said its reclined back placed a tuberculosis patient at the best angle for breathing. The degree of bending pushed wood-working methods of the period to their technical limits. The chair later entered the permanent collections of the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Finnish Design Museum. The Aaltos’ experience designing furnishings for buildings helped lead to the 1935 founding of Artek, which promoted their furniture and glassware and produced furnishings for their architectural projects.

events.title: Develops Paimio Chair
events.description: Alvar and Aino Aalto develop the Paimio Chair for tuberculosis patients in 1931. They create it while designing the interiors and furnishings for Paimio Sanatorium.

event_class.title: Paimio Chair
event_class.description: A cantilevered chair uses laminated birch strips bent into a resilient frame with a curved plywood seat and back.
event_class.impact: Aalto’s bent-plywood furniture influenced the aesthetics of later designers, including Charles and Ray Eames and George Nelson.

events.title: Founds Artek
events.description: In December 1935, Alvar Aalto, Aino Aalto, Maire Gullichsen, and Nils-Gustav Hahl founded Artek in Helsinki to sell Aalto-designed furniture and glassware.

events.title: Designs Villa Mairea
events.description: In 1937, Alvar and Aino Aalto began designing Villa Mairea near Noormarkku for Maire and Harry Gullichsen. The design combined white modernist surfaces with timber columns, brickwork, local materials, and custom furnishings.

images.caption: Alvar Aalto’s Villa Mairea in Noormarkku
images.creator: J-P Kärnä

events.background:
The commission came from a family at the center of Finnish industry. Maire Gullichsen was Walter Ahlström’s daughter and Antti Ahlström’s granddaughter. Harry Gullichsen worked for A. Ahlström Ab. Maire had studied art in Helsinki and Paris. Her training included Fernand Léger’s studio. After her father’s death in 1931, she had the financial independence to support cultural projects. She helped found Helsinki’s Free Art School in 1935. The school followed the model of Paris academies and accepted students without entrance requirements. She also wanted the house to provide a setting for her modern-art collection.

By this time, the Aaltos had spent the 1930s testing laminated wood, abstract reliefs, and irregular curved forms. Those experiments addressed the technical limits of flexible wood. They also fed into the spatial problems of their buildings. Aino concentrated particularly on interiors and furniture during their shared design work. At Artek, she established and revised furniture designs and standards. The villa gave the architects and their client a large private setting in which architecture, furnishings, and art could be considered together.

The house was organized as a U around an inner garden. Its central feature was a kidney-shaped swimming pool. A sauna beside the pool used a deliberately rustic treatment. The plan drew on Finnish and Japanese precedents. Aalto described the project as an experiment with lessons for mass housing. The villa was completed in 1939. It became one of the works for which Aalto is most widely recognized internationally. Maire continued to build institutions for modern art. Her foundation, created in 1971, became the basis of the Pori Art Museum, which opened in 1981.

events.title: Receives MoMA Solo Exhibition
events.description: The Museum of Modern Art in New York presents Aalto: Architecture and Furniture, a solo exhibition of Alvar Aalto’s work. Aalto is the second architect to receive a solo exhibition at the museum.

events.title: Creates Finnish Fair Pavilion
events.description: Aalto designed Finland’s pavilion for the 1939 New York World’s Fair. Its interior featured a tall, curved wooden display wall and exhibits of Finnish industry, art, and design.

images.caption: Interior of Finland’s 1939 World’s Fair pavilion
images.creator: Soller

events.title: Loses Aino Aalto
events.description: Aino Aalto dies of cancer in Helsinki on January 13, 1949.

events.title: Designs Säynätsalo Town Hall
events.description: Aalto’s design for Säynätsalo Town Hall wins the 1949 competition. The complex surrounds an elevated courtyard. It uses red brick, wood, and stepped outdoor spaces.
events.background:
The commission entered Aalto’s office during a period of rebuilding its Finnish practice around public work. Elissa Mäkiniemi graduated from the Helsinki University of Technology in 1949 and joined the office that year. The office was then preparing several competition entries and handling extensive public commissions in Finland and abroad. Mäkiniemi took part in every competition project undertaken by the practice. She later became Alvar Aalto’s wife and used the name Elissa Aalto from 1952.

## A building site and brick

Elissa Aalto’s first major assignment as supervising architect was the Säynätsalo Town Hall construction site. Work on the building continued from 1949 through 1952. A supervising architect follows the design through construction and coordinates its realization on site. Her later supervising roles included projects at the University of Jyväskylä, Maison Louis Carré in France, and the Nordic House in Reykjavík.

The town hall belongs to the group of projects in which Aalto developed an extensive use of red brick after his return from the United States. Baker House at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, completed in 1949, had begun that phase. Aalto subsequently used brick in major Finnish projects including the Helsinki University of Technology campus, the National Pensions Institute building, and Helsinki’s House of Culture. At Säynätsalo, construction produced the building by 1952.

Elissa Aalto continued to work in the office for the rest of Alvar Aalto’s life. After his death in 1976, she directed the practice until 1994. She oversaw the completion of several unfinished Aalto projects and arranged for the office’s drawings, photographs, and documents to pass to the Alvar Aalto Foundation.

events.title: Marries Elissa Mäkiniemi
events.description: Aalto marries architect Elissa Mäkiniemi in 1952. She has worked at his office since 1949.

events.title: Designs Finlandia Hall
events.description: Aalto designs Finlandia Hall in Helsinki in 1962. The building faces Töölö Bay. It is faced in white Carrara marble and includes a large concert hall.

events.title: Death in Helsinki
events.description: Alvar Aalto died in Helsinki on 11 May 1976, aged 78.
